name: Hebrew (Modern)
summary: Modern Hebrew is a Semitic language revived as a spoken mother tongue in the late 19th and 20th centuries and written right to left in a 22-letter consonant alphabet whose vowels are optional points; everyday texts use a full spelling with ו and י and leave many words ambiguous. Its words grow from consonantal roots placed in patterns — seven verb binyanim and many noun mishkalim — and its grammar is built on gender: masculine and feminine in every noun, in “you”, in the present tense (which shows gender and number but not person) and even in the numbers, whose 3–10 forms look reversed. It has a prefixed definite article, and for “a” at most the numeral “one” (אֶחָד), no cases, a construct state for “X of Y”, the object marker אֶת, no present-tense “to be” and no verb “to have”. Small words (and, the, in, to, from, that) are written onto the next word, and the language mixes an ancient literary layer with a direct, informal everyday style that has no polite “you”.
sources: Wiktionary (kaikki.org extracts) — as used for the course lexicon

Lewis Glinert, Modern Hebrew: An Essential Grammar (Routledge)

Avraham Even-Shoshan, the Even-Shoshan dictionary (המילון החדש)

phenomena.title: An alphabet of 22 consonant letters
phenomena.what: Hebrew is written in the square Hebrew script, an abjad: its 22 letters are consonants, and vowels are either left out or added as optional points. Four letters (א ה ו י) also serve as vowel helpers (matres lectionis). The order and names of the letters (alef, bet, gimel, dalet …) go back to the Phoenician alphabet.

examples.note: the first four letters, in the order inherited from the Phoenician alphabet
a word written with consonants only

phenomena.title: Right to left, with numbers left to right
phenomena.what: Hebrew runs from right to left, but numbers written in digits, and any Latin words inside a Hebrew line, run left to right. This mixed (bidirectional) text needs care in typing and in the app layout: punctuation and digits next to Hebrew easily end up on the wrong side.

phenomena.title: Five letters have a final form
phenomena.what: Five letters change shape at the end of a word: כ → ך, מ → ם, נ → ן, פ → ף, צ → ץ. When an ending is added the ordinary form comes back (שֻׁלְחָן → שֻׁלְחָנוֹת). All other letters have one shape in every position, and letters are not joined in print.

examples.text: ך ם ן ף ץ / כ מ נ פ צ
examples.note: final / non-final forms
table → tables: final ן becomes נ before the ending

model.other: The forms are stored correctly in all 476 lexemes and 1241 bank sentences (checked: no final letter inside a word, no non-final letter at the end except the prefix מִ). tools/validate_lang.py does not check it.

phenomena.gap: A validator rule (final form only at the end of a word, except prefixes and abbreviations with geresh), letters.json, and the glyph_form exercise.

phenomena.title: Vowel points (niqqud) and dagesh
phenomena.what: Vowels are dots and dashes under, inside or above the letters: kamats ָ and patach ַ (a), tsere ֵ and segol ֶ (e), chirik ִ (i), cholam ֹ (o), kubuts ֻ and shuruk וּ (u), shva ְ, and the hataf vowels ֲ ֱ ֳ. The dagesh dot inside a letter doubles it or makes ב כ פ hard. Niqqud is used in teaching texts, poetry, children's books and the Bible; ordinary texts leave it out.

examples.note: book, with and without vowel points
teacher (m.) / teacher (f.): only the points tell them apart

phenomena.record: every form is stored fully vocalized (§4.5); the unvocalized spelling is derived by stripping the marks, or given in plene

phenomena.title: A separate handwriting (cursive) script
phenomena.alsoNote: The tag only says the language has one script; a handwriting form whose letters differ strongly from print is the point here. Russian/Cyrillic cursive (т, д, и) is a partial parallel.
phenomena.what: Hebrew has one script, but it is handwritten in a cursive form whose letters often look quite different from print (א, ג, ה, ל, צ and others), and almost nobody handwrites the print letters. A learner who wants to read notes or write by hand must learn both sets of shapes.

examples.note: printed here; in cursive several of these shapes change completely

model.other: No cursive font, template or exercise.

phenomena.gap: A cursive font or stroke templates in letters.json and the trace exercise (self-checked, §6.1); a recognition drill print ↔ cursive.

phenomena.title: No capital letters
phenomena.what: Hebrew has no upper and lower case: names, sentence starts and abbreviations look like any other word. Names are recognised from context (and in learner texts, from the transliteration).

examples.note: Dana lives in Tel Aviv

model.other: language.json capitalizeFirst false; proper names are bank tokens with name: true (§4.8), also after a prefix (וְשָׂרָה).

phenomena.title: Full spelling without vowels (ktiv male)
phenomena.alsoNote: The Academy's full spelling (extra ו/י, doubled consonantal ו/י) is a rule of Hebrew orthography; Arabic, Persian and Urdu write long vowels but have no separate unvocalized spelling standard.
phenomena.what: Ordinary texts use the full spelling of the Academy of the Hebrew Language: without niqqud, extra ו and י are written for o/u and for i (שולחן, כיסא), and a consonantal ו or י inside a word is doubled (הוורוד, סתיו). So the unvocalized word is not simply the vocalized one with the points removed. Learners must read and type this spelling, not the stripped one.

examples.note: ו added for the u vowel
י added for the i vowel
the pink one: a consonantal ו inside the word is doubled

phenomena.record: spelling: the everyday full spelling (ktiv male) of every word (features.spelling); plene: the full spelling of every cell whose everyday spelling is not the stripped vocalized form (cell → spelling); words without forms give it in alts

phenomena.title: One unvocalized spelling, several words
phenomena.what: Without vowels many different words share one spelling, and the reader picks the right one from context: ספר can be a book, counted, told or a barber. Even the full spelling leaves many pairs: את is both the object marker and “you (f.)”, יפה is both יָפֶה and יָפָה.

examples.note: book / counted / told / barber
object marker / you (f.)
brown / heat, fever

model.other: Traps in fn.object (את), fn.adjective (יפה) and fn.prep.core (בבית); the loose tokenizer returns every reading of an unvocalized word. No list of homograph sets.

phenomena.gap: A per-language homograph index (derivable from the form index), an exercise that asks for the reading in context, and the reading in context shown in tap-to-gloss.

phenomena.title: One-letter words written onto the next word
phenomena.alsoNote: Arabic writes وَ فَ بِ لِ كَ and ال onto the next word and stacks them (وبالبيت). French elided l', d', qu' are only a partial parallel.
phenomena.what: Seven small words are single letters attached to the following word: וְ “and”, הַ “the”, בְּ “in”, לְ “to”, מִ “from”, כְּ “as, like” and שֶׁ “that”. Up to three can pile up, so a dictionary word is often hidden behind them: וּבַבַּיִת = and + in + the + house.

examples.note: and in the house — one written word
from the house
that you

phenomena.record: prefix: true on the clitic lexeme, with alts for its other spellings

model.other: prefix (true / false) is stated by every preposition and conjunction (wordFeatures ADP, CCONJ, SCONJ, at the top level); 6 prefix lexemes (וְ, לְ, בְּ, מִ, כְּשֶׁ, שֶׁ) with alts; bank tokens with parts; langcore strips up to two prefixes (longest first) and keeps a prefixed word as one tile. The article הַ is not a lexeme but part of the DEF cells.

phenomena.title: The prefixes change their vowel
phenomena.alsoNote: The vowel changes of וְ בְּ לְ כְּ מִ by the following sound are specific to Hebrew vocalization.
phenomena.what: The prefixes take different vowels by what follows: וְ becomes וּ before a shva and before ב מ פ; בְּ לְ כְּ become בִּ לִ כִּ before a shva and take the article's vowel (בַּבַּיִת); מִ doubles the next letter and becomes מֵ before gutturals and the article. A learner who writes these words with niqqud has to choose the right vowel.

examples.note: in a house / in the house — the article fuses into the prefix
twenty-three: וְ becomes וּ before a shva
from Tel Aviv (next letter doubled) / from Haifa

phenomena.record: the spellings of each prefix (alts) and the form of the word after a prefix (PFX cells)

model.other: alts on he:ve (וּ וַ), he:be, he:min; ADP;DEF / ADP;ALT cells on לְ; 43 nouns have a PFX cell (the noun after a prefix + article). The tokenizer accepts any listed spelling; nothing checks that the right one was chosen.

phenomena.gap: A rule or stored variants for every prefix (בְּ, כְּ, וְ, מִ, שֶׁ) and a check that a bank token uses the right one; a choose-the-prefix-vowel drill (vowelize).

phenomena.title: Geresh, gershayim and maqaf
phenomena.alsoNote: Geresh/gershayim for acronyms, letter numerals and loan sounds are Hebrew conventions; Persian and Urdu add new dotted letters (پ چ ژ گ) instead.
phenomena.what: The geresh ׳ and the gershayim ״ mark abbreviations and acronyms (צה״ל, read as a word), letters used as numbers (ט״ו), and — on ג ז צ — the sounds [dʒ], [ʒ] and [tʃ] of loanwords (ג׳ ז׳ צ׳), for which the alphabet has no letter. The maqaf ־ is a high hyphen that joins words, above all the two nouns of a construct pair in vocalized texts. The other punctuation marks are the common Latin-script ones (. , ? ! : and quotation marks).

examples.note: IDF — an acronym read as a word
pyjamas — ג׳ is the sound j
school — maqaf in a vocalized construct pair

model.other: Not described; the tokenizer has no rule for ׳ ״ inside a word.

phenomena.gap: A script page on geresh/gershayim/maqaf, tokenizer support for acronyms and letters with geresh, and abbreviation entries (ת״א, וכו׳) in the lexicon.

phenomena.title: No single romanization
phenomena.alsoNote: Competing romanizations that hide letters with the same sound exist for Arabic, Persian and Urdu; other non-Latin scripts (ru, el, hi) also have several systems, but the tagged value (one script) occurs in Latin-script languages that have no such problem.
phenomena.what: Hebrew is romanized in several ways (ch / kh / h for ח and כ, ' or nothing for א and ע, e or ei for ֵי). A learner relying on transliteration must know that one sound can be spelled several ways and that the Latin spelling hides the difference between letters that sound alike.

examples.note: the same sound [χ] is written ch in one course word and kh in another

phenomena.record: translit: one consistent learner romanization per word (wordFeatures, at the top level, with the scheme in its “why”)

model.other: Every lexeme has translit, normalized to one scheme (written in the translit declaration of wordFeatures): ch for ח and כ (no kh), ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי (eifo, ein, eich, bein), ai for ַי (ulai, matai), one ASCII apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word (na'im, sha'a, mis'ada), a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-, ve-, she-). Ids stay as they were (he:sabim is read savim).

phenomena.gap: A validator check of the scheme; stress is not marked (see he.phon.stress).

phenomena.title: Letters as numbers (gematria)
phenomena.alsoNote: Greek alphabetic numerals (α΄ β΄ … ι΄ κ΄ … ρ΄) work the same way and are still used for lists, chapters and rulers, though not for calendar dates; Arabic abjad numerals exist but are rare.
phenomena.what: Each letter has a number value (א 1 … י 10, כ 20 … ק 100 … ת 400), added up within a decimal system. These numerals are used for Jewish calendar dates and years, for chapters and lists, and on official documents beside the digits.

examples.note: (5)787 — the Jewish year that began in September 2026: ת 400 + ש 300 + פ 80 + ז 7
the 15th of Shevat: 15 is written 9 + 6, not 10 + 5

model.other: Not in the course.

phenomena.gap: A numbers page (letters → values, the 15/16 rule, years without the thousands) and a number_words drill for Hebrew-letter numerals.

phenomena.title: Five vowels, no vowel length
phenomena.what: Modern Hebrew has five vowels — a, e, i, o, u — and the length of a vowel never distinguishes words. The many vowel signs are a legacy of older Hebrew: kamats and patach are both a, tsere and segol both e; the kamats katan (ׇ) is o.

examples.note: patach and kamats sound the same
two months — kamats katan is o

model.other: Overview fact “Sounds”; translit shows the vowels; kamats katan is written ׇ (U+05C7) where it occurs. No audio.

phenomena.gap: Audio (P9) and the letters.json sound table; a transliterate drill.

phenomena.title: No vowel harmony: endings keep their vowels
phenomena.what: Suffixes do not adapt their vowels to the vowels of the stem: the plural endings -ִים and -וֹת, the feminine -ָה and -ֶת and the person endings of the verb have the same vowels after any stem. Vowels change inside the stem instead (by pattern and when the stress moves), and the one-letter prefixes change their vowel by the consonant that follows (בְּ / בִּ / בַּ), which is a rule of the prefix, not harmony.

examples.note: books, songs, horses: -im after any stem vowel
big (f.), small (f.): the same -a after o and after a

phenomena.title: No front rounded vowels (ü, ö)
phenomena.what: The five vowels a, e, i, o, u include no front rounded vowels: lip rounding goes only with the back vowels o and u. Names and loanwords with ü or ö are said and spelled with i or u, e or o.

examples.note: Zürich — ü is said as i
Goethe — ö is said as e

phenomena.title: No nasal vowels
phenomena.what: Vowels are always oral: a vowel before n or m stays an oral vowel followed by a full consonant, and no word is distinguished by nasality. Loanwords with nasal vowels are said with a vowel + n or m.

examples.note: restaurant — the nasal vowel of the source becomes -an
champagne — a vowel + m

phenomena.title: Consonants: [χ], uvular [ʁ], [ts], voiced and voiceless pairs
phenomena.what: ח and soft כ are both the uvular fricative [χ]; ר is a uvular [ʁ]; צ is the affricate [ts]. Voiced and voiceless consonants are distinct in stops and fricatives (b / p, d / t, g / k, v / f, z / s), and r and l are separate sounds. Standard Israeli Hebrew has lost the old pharyngeals: ע is said like א (a glottal stop or nothing) and ח like כ — though many speakers of Mizrahi background still keep them. Geresh letters add [dʒ], [ʒ] and [tʃ] for loanwords.

examples.note: street: uvular [ʁ] and [χ]
yellow: צ = ts

model.other: Overview fact “Sounds”; no audio, no letters.json.

phenomena.gap: letters.json with sounds per letter, audio (P9).

phenomena.title: No ejectives or implosives
phenomena.what: All consonants are made with ordinary air from the lungs: there are no ejectives (p', t', k') and no implosives. The letters ט and ק, once 'emphatic' consonants, are now plain t and k, the same sounds as ת and כּ.

examples.note: good / queue: ט and ת are the same plain t
cold / pillow: ק and כּ are the same plain k

phenomena.title: No click consonants
phenomena.what: Clicks are not consonants of the language: no word contains one. Every consonant, including the affricate צ [ts], is made with air going out.

examples.note: yellow: צ is the affricate [ts], made with outgoing air

phenomena.title: No retroflex consonants
phenomena.what: t, d, n, l, s, ts and sh are made with the tongue tip or blade at the teeth or the gum ridge; no consonant is made with the tip curled back, and no pair of words differs that way.

examples.note: six: ש is [ʃ], said with the tongue blade, not curled back
fish: one d, at the teeth or gum ridge

phenomena.title: Aspiration does not distinguish words
phenomena.what: p, t and k are said with little or no puff of air, and adding or dropping a puff never makes another word. Stops are kept apart by voicing instead: b / p, d / t, g / k.

examples.note: here / in him: voicing, not aspiration, separates the words
dew / poor

phenomena.title: No final devoicing
phenomena.what: Voiced consonants keep their voicing at the end of a word, so a final g, d, z or v can distinguish words from their voiceless partners.

examples.note: fish / thin: final g and k are different
gas / rude: final z and s are different

phenomena.title: No long consonants: the doubling dot is silent
phenomena.what: Consonant length does not distinguish words. Vocalized texts still show the old doubling with a dagesh dot (אִמָּא, הַסֵּפֶר), and some patterns (pi‘el, קַטָּל) are defined by it, but the consonant is said short; in ב כ פ the dot only shows the hard sound.

examples.note: mum: written with a doubling dot, said with one m
told / counted: the dot changes f to p, not the length

phenomena.gap: The overview notes (ja, fi) say that the dagesh never lengthens a consonant; the P4 script module (niqqud) still has to say it.

phenomena.title: No “th” sounds (θ, ð)
phenomena.what: There are no interdental fricatives: the soft ת and ד, which once had these sounds, are now said t and d. Loanwords with θ are said with t.

examples.note: theatre — θ is said t
mathematics

phenomena.title: No hard and soft consonant pairs
phenomena.what: Consonants do not come in plain and palatalised ('soft') pairs: a y-sound is a separate consonant (י), and a consonant before i or e is not softened in a way that changes words.

examples.note: to me: an ordinary l before i
paper: n + y are two consonants, not a soft n

phenomena.title: Letters that sound the same
phenomena.alsoNote: Persian and Urdu have the same kind of merged Arabic letters (ث س ص = s, ت ط = t, ح ه = h, ء ع); Greek has several letters and digraphs for one sound (ι η υ ει οι = i, ο ω = o). English and French spelling are partial parallels.
phenomena.what: Because old sound distinctions merged, several letters now share one sound: א and ע (glottal stop or silent), ב and ו (v), ח and כ ([χ]), ט and ת (t), כּ and ק (k), ס and שׂ (s). The once pharyngeal ח and ע and the once 'emphatic' ט and ק are now plain consonants. The spelling of every word must therefore be learned with the word; related words in other Semitic languages, which often keep these sounds apart, can show which letter is right.

examples.note: tea / good: ת and ט are both t
ס and שׂ are both s
כּ and ק are both k

model.other: Not taught; the planned spell exercise would train it.

phenomena.gap: A script page on homophonous letters, the spell exercise with letter-level feedback (§6.1), and cognate hints from Arabic (bridges).

phenomena.title: Hard and soft b/v, k/kh, p/f (begadkefat)
phenomena.alsoNote: A hard/soft alternation of b k p written with a dot is specific to Hebrew; Spanish has postvocalic softening of b d g only as allophones, never spelled.
phenomena.what: ב כ פ have two sounds: hard (with dagesh) b k p, soft v kh f. The soft sound appears after a vowel, so the same root letter alternates inside one paradigm and after a prefix: כָּתַב / יִכְתֹּב, בַּיִת / בְּבַיִת. Loanwords usually keep their hard sound (בַּפַּארְק “in the park”), and colloquial speech levels some alternations.

examples.note: house → in a house
wrote → will write: k ↔ kh and v ↔ b in one root
a loanword keeps p after the prefix

phenomena.record: carried by the vocalized forms (dagesh) and the PFX cells; nothing extra per word

model.other: The dagesh is stored in every vocalized form; overview fact on bet/vet, kaf/khaf, pe/fe; trap in fn.prep.time (בְּדֵצֶמְבֶּר).

phenomena.gap: A phonology page with the rule and its exceptions (loanwords, colloquial levelling), and a transliterate/reading drill that checks b/v, k/kh, p/f.

phenomena.title: No grammatical consonant mutation
phenomena.what: The first consonant of a word does not change to mark grammar such as possession, gender or case. The one regular alternation, b / v, k / χ, p / f (begadkefat), depends on the sound before the consonant (a vowel or not) and on the word's pattern, not on a grammatical trigger word, and loanwords keep their hard sound.

examples.note: my house / her house: the noun does not change for the possessor
house → in a house: b becomes v after the vowel of the prefix — a sound rule

phenomena.title: Stress: mostly final, but distinctive
phenomena.what: Most words are stressed on the last syllable (milra), but segolate nouns (יֶלֶד yéled, בֹּקֶר bóker), many loanwords and some suffixes take penultimate stress (mil'el). Stress can separate words spelled the same, and niqqud does not show it.

examples.note: food / eats
he wanted / she ran
child — segolates are stressed on the first syllable

phenomena.record: stress: the stressed syllable of the lemma (final / penultimate), and of any form where it moves

model.other: No stress data; translit carries no accent.

phenomena.gap: A stress field (or an accent in translit) for every content word, a validator default (final) with exceptions, and use in TTS (P9).

phenomena.title: No lexical tone: pitch never changes a word
phenomena.what: Hebrew has no lexical tone and no pitch accent: a word keeps its meaning whatever the pitch of its syllables. Pitch belongs to the sentence — a final rise makes a yes/no question, a fall ends a statement — and to emotion and emphasis. A word is identified by its consonants, its vowels and its stressed syllable, and the script accordingly has no tone marks.

examples.note: you want coffee — falling pitch: a statement
do you want coffee? — the same words with a final rise: pitch changes the sentence, never a word

phenomena.title: Gutturals: א ה ח ע ר
phenomena.alsoNote: The rule that gutturals cannot double and take a-vowels is a Hebrew (Tiberian) rule; the tagged stem changes do not imply it.
phenomena.what: The gutturals cannot be doubled and prefer a-vowels and hataf vowels. So the article becomes הָ or הֶ instead of doubling (הָאִשָּׁה, הֶחָבֵר), and verbs whose root has a guttural change their vowels (לֶאֱכֹל, אוֹהֲבִים). Many irregular-looking forms follow from this one rule.

examples.note: the article doubles the next letter, but not a guttural
to eat: hataf segol under א

phenomena.record: carried by the vocalized forms

model.other: fn.definite explains the article before gutturals; fn.root.pattern mentions hataf vowels; every form is stored.

phenomena.gap: The guttural rules as a decision procedure for verbs (part of the weak-root classes), and the vowelize exercise.

phenomena.title: The “stolen” patach before final ח and ע
phenomena.alsoNote: Specific to Hebrew pronunciation and vocalization.
phenomena.what: After a long vowel, a word-final ח, ע (or ה with a dot) is preceded by a short a that is written under the last letter but pronounced before it: תַּפּוּחַ is tapúach, not tapuch. Many common words end like this (שָׁבוּעַ, מַפְתֵּחַ, שָׂמֵחַ, מַדּוּעַ).

examples.note: apple
week
tall — ה with a dot (mappiq) is a consonant

model.other: Stored in the forms and the transliterations; not explained anywhere.

phenomena.gap: A reading rule in the script module and a reading drill.

phenomena.title: Shva and word-initial clusters
phenomena.what: The shva ְ is usually silent in Modern Hebrew, so words can start with two consonants (גְּבִינָה gvina, כְּפָר kfar, סְפִינָה sfina), and a vowel of the stem drops when an ending moves the stress (סֵפֶר → סְפָרִים). An e is heard in some cases — after the one-letter prefixes and often when the first consonant is מ, נ, ל, ר or י (מְנוֹרָה menora).

examples.note: cheese: a cluster at the start
lamp: here an e is heard

model.other: The transliterations show the actual pronunciation; no rule is taught.

phenomena.gap: A reading rule (shva na / nach as said today) in the script module and a transliterate drill.

phenomena.title: Roots of three consonants
phenomena.what: Most native words are built on a root of (usually) three consonants that carries a core meaning: א־כ־ל “eat” gives אָכַל “ate”, אוֹכֵל “eats”, אֹכֶל “food”, מַאֲכָל “dish”. Knowing the root lets the learner guess new words and find them in a dictionary, many of which are ordered by root. Loanwords (סָלָט, טֶלֶפוֹן) have no Semitic root.

examples.note: ate, eats, food, dish
pupil — “one who learns”

phenomena.record: root: the root letters separated by spaces (א כ ל), or none with the reason (loanword, compound, primary or unknown-origin word)

model.other: root on every noun (141 of 258 with a root, the rest none with the reason), every adjective (43 of 45) and all 19 verbs; shown on the word card (facade) and by langcore principalParts.

phenomena.gap: A validator check of the root format and the root_family / root_pattern exercises (§6.2, §6.3); roots for the adverbs and function words are not stated.

phenomena.title: Fusional words: roots, patterns, mostly suffixes
phenomena.what: Grammatical meanings are packed together: one ending or pattern carries several at once (-וֹת = feminine + plural; the present form אוֹכֶלֶת = present + feminine + singular), and stems change inside by root and pattern. Inflection is mostly at the end of the word — the plural, the past-tense person endings, the possessive and prepositional endings — but some grammar comes first: the future marks person with prefixes (אֶ־, תִּ־, יִ־, נִ־), and the article and the one-letter prepositions are written at the front.

examples.note: we ate: one ending, -nu, says 1st person + plural
we will eat: in the future the person is a prefix
cars: -ot is feminine + plural in one piece

phenomena.title: Roots of four consonants
phenomena.what: Some roots have four consonants, many of them made from loanwords: טֶלֶפוֹן “phone” → טִלְפֵּן “he phoned” (ט־ל־פ־נ). They are conjugated in the piel-type patterns (pi‘el, pu‘al, hitpa‘el), which makes them the regular way to turn a borrowed noun into a verb.

examples.note: phone → he phoned (root ט־ל־פ־נ)
engineer — root ה־נ־ד־ס (Arabic handasa)

phenomena.record: root with four letters

model.other: Four-letter roots are stated in features.root: גַּרְגִּיר, כַּרְפַּס, מְהַנְדֵּס, מְהַנְדֶּסֶת, פִּלְפֵּל, שְׂמֹאל; no quadriliteral verb yet.

phenomena.gap: A note in fn.root.pattern, and the quadriliteral verbs (pi‘el / hitpa‘el) when they come; the rootClass value “quadriliteral” is declared for them.

phenomena.title: Seven verb patterns (binyanim)
phenomena.what: Every verb belongs to one of seven patterns: pa‘al, nif‘al, pi‘el, pu‘al, hif‘il, huf‘al, hitpa‘el. The binyan fixes all the forms of the verb (past, present, future, infinitive) and often its meaning in relation to the same root: active, passive, causative, reflexive or reciprocal. A verb is learned with its binyan.

examples.note: went in / put in / convened / gathered — root כ־נ־ס in four binyanim
goodbye — literally “to see each other” (hitpa‘el of ר־א־ה)

phenomena.record: binyan: one of paal, nifal, piel, pual, hifil, hufal, hitpael (a string, values listed in the declaration)

phenomena.title: Weak roots (gizrot)
phenomena.what: Roots with a weak letter change shape in predictable ways: a final ה drops or becomes ת (שָׁתָה → לִשְׁתּוֹת), a middle ו/י leaves only two letters (בָּא, רָץ), a first נ is swallowed and doubles the next letter (נ־ג־ע → הִגִּיעַ), a first י shows up only in some forms (יָצָא → לָצֵאת), and gutturals change the vowels. The class (gizra) explains most “irregular” verbs.

examples.note: drank → drinks (f.) → to drink: final ה drops or becomes ת
comes → comes (f.); runs → runs (f.): hollow roots show two letters
arrived: the נ is assimilated (doubled ג)

phenomena.record: rootClass: the weak classes of the root (e.g. lamed-he, ayin-vav, pe-nun, pe-yod, guttural), or “regular”

model.other: rootClass on all 34 verbs (regular, pe-nun, pe-yod, ayin-vav, ayin-yod, ayin-guttural, lamed-he, lamed-guttural, irregular …); fn.past and fn.future (cr.01, cr.03) show hollow קָם / יָקוּם, pe-yod יָשַׁן / יִישַׁן, the merged נ of יָשַׁנּוּ and the guttural vowels of רָחֲצָה, שׁוֹכַחַת; all forms are stored.

phenomena.title: Noun patterns (mishkalim)
phenomena.what: Nouns and adjectives also follow patterns, and many patterns carry a meaning: מִקְטָל places (מִטְבָּח, מִשְׂרָד), קַטָּל professions (טַבָּח), מַקְטֵל tools (מַפְתֵּחַ), קֶטֶל segolates (יֶלֶד, סֵפֶר), קָטֹל colours (אָדֹם). The pattern also predicts the plural and the construct form.

examples.note: kitchen, office — מִקְטָל: places
cook — קַטָּל: professions
key — מַקְטֵל: tools

phenomena.record: pattern (mishkal) written with the dummy root ק־ט־ל, or none with the reason (loanword, compound, one-syllable or primary noun, suffix formation)

model.other: pattern on every noun (104 of 258 with a pattern), from Wiktionary where it gives one; shown on the word card (facade). One-syllable nouns say none (אֵם, עֵט, יוֹם …): Wiktionary files some of them (אֵם, עוֹף, דּוֹד) under the segolate type they come from, which the reason mentions. מִטָּה keeps מִקְטָלָה (Wiktionary; the radical ה of נ־ט־ה merges with the ending).

phenomena.gap: A meaning label for each pattern (place, tool, profession …) and root_pattern drills.

phenomena.title: Verbs are listed by their past “he” form
phenomena.what: Dictionaries list a Hebrew verb by its past tense 3rd person masculine singular — the shortest form, closest to the root — not by an infinitive: אָכַל “he ate” stands for “to eat”. Hollow verbs look the same in the past and the present (בָּא “came / comes”).

examples.note: “he ate” — the dictionary form of “to eat”
came / comes (m.): past and present share one form

phenomena.record: lemma = V;PST;3;SG;MASC (citation cell)

model.other: language.json citationCells VERB = V;PST;3;SG;MASC, enforced by the validator.

phenomena.title: Two genders, marked and unmarked
phenomena.what: Every noun is masculine or feminine (no neuter). Endings in stressed -ָה and in -ת usually mean feminine, but there are exceptions both ways: כּוֹס “glass” and עִיר “city” are feminine without an ending, לַיְלָה “night” is masculine despite its -ָה. Paired body parts are mostly feminine.

examples.note: glass, night, city — the ending misleads

phenomena.record: gender: MASC or FEM

model.other: gender required on every noun by the validator (GENDERED_NOUNS); 258 nouns carry it; gender_article drills it.

phenomena.title: Masculine and feminine nouns for people
phenomena.what: Nouns for people come in pairs: the feminine adds -ָה, -ֶת or -ִית to the masculine (מוֹרֶה / מוֹרָה, נֶהָג / נַהֶגֶת, סְטוּדֶנְט / סְטוּדֶנְטִית). The pair exists for almost every job and person, and the masculine plural is used for mixed groups.

examples.note: teacher (m./f.)
student (m./f.)
driver (m./f.)

phenomena.record: the two words share the concept and say what separates them (contrasts, axis “gender of the person”)

model.other: The two words are separate lexemes with the same concept (he:more / he:mora); their contrasts (axis “gender of the person”) link them. langcore principalParts looks for a cell N;SG;FEM;INDF that Hebrew lexemes never have, so the card shows the pair only through the concept.

phenomena.gap: The counterpart on the word card and a “make the feminine” drill.

phenomena.title: Plurals in -ִים and -וֹת
phenomena.what: Masculine nouns usually take -ִים, feminine -וֹת, but the ending does not prove the gender: חַלּוֹן → חַלּוֹנוֹת is masculine, אִשָּׁה → נָשִׁים feminine. A few common nouns are irregular (בַּיִת → בָּתִּים, אָחוֹת → אֲחָיוֹת). Agreement always follows the gender of the singular.

examples.note: window: masculine with -ot
woman: feminine with -im and a new stem
house → houses

phenomena.record: plurals: the plural form(s) with their kind (-im / -ot / irregular) and the senses they belong to

model.other: plurals on every noun: the form, its ending (im / ot: a mismatch with the gender is visible) and the meanings it belongs to, with a note where a meaning has its own plural or only the plural (16 nouns: כִּכָּרוֹת / כִּכְּרוֹת, נְיָרוֹת, בָּנִים, נְכָדִים …); none with the reason for mass, plural-only and month nouns. The cells N;PL;INDF / N;PL;DEF hold the forms; fn.plural.noun lists an “agree” generator, which langcore does not implement (ignored).

phenomena.title: Vowel changes in the stem
phenomena.what: When an ending is added the stress moves and earlier vowels shorten or disappear: סֵפֶר → סְפָרִים, גָּדוֹל → גְּדוֹלָה. Segolate nouns (קֶטֶל) change their whole vowel pattern, and short adjectives double their last letter (קָטָן → קְטַנָּה).

examples.note: book → books
big (m. → f.)
small (m. → f.): the נ doubles

phenomena.record: carried by the stored forms

model.other: All forms stored; the traps of fn.plural.noun and fn.adjective explain the shortening.

phenomena.title: The dual -ַיִם
phenomena.what: A dual ending -ַיִם means “two” of a few units of time and of 100 and 1000 (יוֹמַיִם “two days”, מָאתַיִם “200”). For paired body parts the dual is simply the plural (יָדַיִם “hands”, also for more than two), and some nouns exist only in this form (מַיִם “water”, מִשְׁקָפַיִם “glasses”, אוֹפַנַּיִם “bicycle”). It is not productive: other nouns say “two” with the number and the plural (שְׁנֵי סְפָרִים).

examples.note: two days
hands — the dual is the plural of paired body parts
glasses — dual in form, plural only

phenomena.record: dual: the dual form when the noun has one in use, or none

model.other: dual on every noun: the form (with its meanings) for 6 nouns (יוֹמַיִם, שְׁבוּעַיִם, חׇדְשַׁיִם, שְׁנָתַיִם, שְׁעָתַיִם, דְּלָתַיִם), none with the reason for the rest; N;DU;INDF on 5 time nouns, NUM;DU on מֵאָה / אֶלֶף; מַיִם, אוֹפַנַּיִם, צָהֳרַיִם say that they only look like duals.

phenomena.gap: Body-part nouns (when the body field comes) with dual = plural, and the rule that for these nouns the dual is preferred to שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + plural.

phenomena.title: No numeral classifiers: numbers count nouns directly
phenomena.what: A numeral stands directly before the noun it counts: שְׁלוֹשָׁה סְפָרִים “three books”. There are no measure words chosen by the shape or kind of the thing; a unit is needed only for a mass, and then it is an ordinary noun in a construct pair (שְׁתֵּי כּוֹסוֹת קָפֶה “two cups of coffee”).

examples.note: two books: the number + the plural noun
two cups of coffee: a unit only for a mass

phenomena.title: Plural-only, singular-only and mass nouns
phenomena.what: Some nouns have no singular (אֲנָשִׁים “people”, מַיִם “water”, הוֹרִים “parents”), some count nouns lack a plural and borrow it from another word (אָדָם → אֲנָשִׁים), and food words are often mass nouns used in the singular (קָנִיתִי גֶּזֶר “I bought carrots”). A few mass nouns have a feminine noun for one piece (שֵׂעָר “hair” → שַׂעֲרָה “a single hair”), but this is not a productive process.

examples.note: people — plural only
water — always plural
garlic — a mass noun

phenomena.record: class: plt / sgt / mass / cal, or none for an ordinary count noun

model.other: language.json classes NOUN.plt (6), NOUN.sgt (7), NOUN.mass (41), NOUN.cal (18), each with its own paradigmCells checked by the validator.

phenomena.title: No cases: a noun has one form in every role
phenomena.what: Nouns, adjectives and pronouns do not change their ending for their role in the sentence: הַיֶּלֶד is the same as subject, as object and after a preposition. Roles are shown by word order (subject before the verb), by אֶת before a definite direct object, by prepositions (mostly one-letter prefixes) and by the agreement of the verb. A pronoun as object or after a preposition is the preposition with a personal ending (אוֹתִי, לִי).

examples.text: הַיֶּלֶד פֹּה / אֲנִי רוֹאֶה אֶת הַיֶּלֶד / אֲנִי עִם הַיֶּלֶד
examples.translit: hayeled po / ani ro'e et hayeled / ani im hayeled
examples.note: the boy is here / I see the boy / I am with the boy: one form in three roles
in / to / from the city: only the preposition changes

phenomena.title: The definite article הַ, and “one” for “a”
phenomena.what: “The” is the prefix הַ, which doubles the next consonant and changes its vowel before gutturals (הָאִשָּׁה, הֶחָבֵר). A bare noun is indefinite, and there is no separate indefinite article; in speech the numeral “one”, אֶחָד / אַחַת after the noun, often serves as one (“a certain”: בָּחוּר אֶחָד). Names, nouns with a possessive suffix and the first noun of a construct pair take no article.

examples.note: a book → the book
a woman → the woman

phenomena.record: the DEF cells of every noun and adjective

model.other: Every noun and adjective stores its DEF cells; absent entries for det.def and det.indef explain what Hebrew does instead.

phenomena.title: The construct state (smichut)
phenomena.what: Two nouns are joined “X of Y” by putting the first in a short construct form and the second after it: בַּיִת → בֵּית סֵפֶר “school (house of book)”. Only the first noun changes (-ָה → -ַת, -ִים → -ֵי, vowels shorten); the article goes on the second noun (בֵּית הַסֵּפֶר “the school”); the plural goes on the first (בָּתֵּי סֵפֶר); an adjective comes at the end.

examples.note: house → school
the school — the article on the second noun
schools — only the first noun changes
meal → breakfast: -ָה becomes -ַת

phenomena.record: construct: the singular and plural construct forms of every noun (also stored as the cells N;SG;CONST and N;PL;CONST, compared with Wiktionary), or none with the reason (compound lexemes, month and day names, name-like family words)

model.other: 194 of 258 nouns state their construct forms, all stored as cells (219 of them confirmed by Wiktionary, the rest by the rules of the pattern); compounds (בֵּית סֵפֶר, אֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר) are separate multi-word lexemes and say none. The construct forms of numerals are stored (NUM;…;CONST). There is no grammar function for the construct yet.

phenomena.title: “Of” as a separate word: שֶׁל
phenomena.what: The everyday way to link a possessor to a noun is the word שֶׁל “of”, placed after the possessed noun: הַבַּיִת שֶׁל דָּנָה “Dana's house”. The possessed noun comes first and usually takes the article; שֶׁל takes personal endings for pronoun possessors (שֶׁלִּי, שֶׁלְּךָ, שֶׁלָּהּ …). Beside it stand the construct state (fixed pairs and formal style) and the possessive endings.

examples.note: Dana's house
my book

phenomena.title: Possessive endings on nouns
phenomena.what: Besides the everyday הַבַּיִת שֶׁלִּי, a noun can take a possessive ending: אָחִי “my brother”, אִשְׁתִּי “my wife”. There are two sets: one for singular nouns (-ִי, -ְךָ, -וֹ …) and one for plural nouns (-ַי, -ֶיךָ, -ָיו …). In speech the endings live on a few family words; in writing they are common. A noun with an ending is definite.

examples.note: my brother
my wife: the construct stem אִשְׁתּ־
my parents: the endings for plural nouns

phenomena.record: possSuffix: everyday / formal / none, with the N;POSS cells (and N;PL;POSS for countable nouns)

model.other: 13 nouns have the 10 N;POSS cells (singular only); the bank has a Formality variant (שֶׁלִּי ↔ suffix).

phenomena.gap: Plural-possessed forms (אַחַי “my brothers”, יְלָדַי), a register value per noun saying whether the suffix is used in speech, and the possessed forms of more nouns for reading.

phenomena.title: One kind of possession for every noun
phenomena.what: “My X” is built the same way for every kind of noun — body parts, relatives and objects alike: X שֶׁלִּי, or in formal style a possessive ending. In everyday speech the endings are commoner with a few relatives (אִשְׁתִּי, אָחִי), but this is a matter of style and vocabulary, not of grammar, and שֶׁל is always possible.

examples.text: הַיָּד שֶׁלִּי / הָאָח שֶׁלִּי / הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁלִּי
examples.translit: hayad sheli / ha'akh sheli / hasefer sheli
examples.note: my hand / my brother / my book: one construction

phenomena.title: Prepositions with personal endings
phenomena.alsoNote: Arabic (لي، بك، عليه), Irish (agam, liom) and Welsh (ataf, arnaf) inflect prepositions for person. Hungarian personal forms of postpositions and case endings (nekem, velem) are a partial parallel.
phenomena.what: Prepositions take personal endings instead of a pronoun: לִי “to me”, בִּשְׁבִילִי “for me”. Some change their stem (עִם → אִתִּי “with me”, מִן → מִמֶּנִּי “from me, than me”, אֶת → אוֹתִי “me”), and some take the plural-noun endings (עַל → עָלַי, לִפְנֵי → לְפָנַי).

examples.note: to me, to you (m.), to you (f.)
with me — a different stem
from me, than me
on me — the endings of plural nouns

phenomena.record: pronForms: the 10 person forms of every preposition (ADP;1;SG …), or none with the reason

model.other: 16 of 31 prepositions state their 10 forms with personal endings (from Wiktionary’s tables: אִתִּי, מִמֶּנִּי, אוֹתִי, עָלַי …); the others say none (שֶׁלִּי … are themselves such forms; time words). phenomena.title: The present: four forms by gender and number
phenomena.alsoNote: A present tense that is an old participle, inflected only for gender and number, is Hebrew's own; the Russian and Ukrainian past (ел, ела, ели) works the same way in another tense, and Hindi-Urdu participle tenses agree in gender and number but add an auxiliary for person.
phenomena.what: The present tense is an old participle and changes like an adjective, for gender and number only: אוֹכֵל, אוֹכֶלֶת, אוֹכְלִים, אוֹכְלוֹת. אֲנִי, אַתָּה and הוּא share one form, so the subject pronoun is required.

examples.note: eats: m. sg / f. sg / m. pl / f. pl — no person

phenomena.record: the four V;PRS cells

model.other: Required cells for every VERB (paradigmCells); bank variants Gender, Number, Addressee.

phenomena.title: The past: person endings
phenomena.what: The past adds endings for person, number and (in the 2nd and 3rd person singular and 2nd plural) gender: אָכַלְתִּי, אָכַלְתָּ, אָכַלְתְּ, אָכַל, אָכְלָה … Because the ending shows the person, the pronoun is often left out in the 1st and 2nd person.

examples.note: I / you (m.) / you (f.) / he / she ate
