phenomena.title: No object marking on the verb in speech
phenomena.what: The verb does not agree with its object: an object pronoun is a separate word, אֶת with a personal ending (רָאִיתִי אוֹתוֹ “I saw him”). Formal and literary writing can still attach an object ending to the verb (רְאִיתִיו “I saw him”), but this is a written style, never doubled with a noun.

examples.note: I saw him: the pronoun is a separate word
I saw him: literary, with the old object ending

phenomena.gap: fn.object teaches אוֹתוֹ; the literary object endings (רְאִיתִיו) are not taught.

phenomena.title: The future: prefixes and endings
phenomena.alsoNote: Arabic and Amharic mark person with the same prefixes (ʔ- t- y- n-), with one form for 'you (m.)' and 'she'; there the prefix conjugation is the imperfect / non-past, not a future only.
phenomena.what: The future marks the person with prefixes (א־, ת־, י־, נ־) and some endings. The same form serves “you (m.)” and “she” (תֹּאכַל). It is also the everyday form of commands and requests, it follows אַל in prohibitions, and it is used after כְּשֶׁ / אִם for future events. The feminine plural forms (תֵּלַכְנָה) are literary; speech uses the masculine plural.

examples.note: I / you (m.) / you (f.) / he / she will eat — “you (m.)” and “she” are one form

phenomena.record: future: the 3rd person masculine singular future of every verb as a principal part (features.future); the 2nd person future cells for commands

model.other: cr.03 realizes fn.future (the prefixes אֶ / תִּ / יִ / נִ, one form for “you (m.)” and “she”, the vowels per binyan, אַל + future, the present and הוֹלֵךְ + infinitive for plans). The 15 verbs of cr.01–cr.03 store the 8 future cells in use (from Wiktionary; the nifʿal 1st person singular is left out, see the lexeme); הָיָה has the 1st and 3rd persons.

phenomena.gap: The foundation verbs (fd.07, fd.13) store only the 2nd person future; the literary feminine plural in ־נָה is described but not stored; the nifʿal 1st person singular (אֵרָדֵם — Wiktionary’s table has אֶרָדֵם) is left out until checked.

phenomena.title: Imperative, future as command, and אַל
phenomena.alsoNote: Arabic also forms the imperative by dropping the prefix of the prefix conjugation and negates commands with لا + jussive. Spanish and Greek prohibitions with a non-imperative form (no vayas, μην πας) are a partial parallel.
phenomena.what: The imperative is the future without its prefix (תֵּלֵךְ → לֵךְ!), with forms for a man, a woman and a group. In speech the future itself is often the command and sounds softer. A prohibition is אַל + future, never the imperative; signs use the infinitive (לֹא לְהִכָּנֵס “no entry”).

examples.note: you will go → go!
don't go!
no entry

phenomena.record: the V;IMP cells (2 sg m, 2 sg f, 2 pl)

model.other: 15 verbs store imperative and 2nd-person future cells; he:al-imp (אַל) has a role; bank variants Mood, Polarity, Formality, Addressee.

phenomena.title: The infinitive with לְ
phenomena.what: The infinitive carries the prefix לְ (לֶאֱכֹל, לִשְׁתּוֹת, לְבַשֵּׁל) and follows verbs such as רוֹצֶה “want”, אוֹהֵב “like”, the impersonal modals (צָרִיךְ, אֶפְשָׁר, אָסוּר), and is used in instructions. Its shape depends on the binyan and the root class.

examples.note: wants to eat
to drink, to cook

phenomena.record: V;NFIN

model.other: V;NFIN is a required cell of every verb.

phenomena.title: Verbal nouns by binyan
phenomena.what: Every binyan has its own action-noun pattern (shem pe‘ula): pa‘al often קְטִילָה (אֲכִילָה “eating”), pi‘el קִטּוּל (בִּשּׁוּל “cooking”), hif‘il הַקְטָלָה (הַגָּעָה “arrival”), hitpa‘el הִתְקַטְּלוּת. It is predictable from the binyan, but whether a verb has one, and what it means, must be checked word by word.

examples.note: ate → eating
cooked → cooking
arrived → arrival

phenomena.record: verbalNoun: the action noun of every verb (features.verbalNoun), or none with the reason

model.other: 15 of 19 verbs state their verbal noun (אֲכִילָה, נְסִיעָה, הַגָּעָה …); the others say why there is none in everyday use (רָצָה, הָיָה, בָּא, חִכָּה). Shown on the word card.

phenomena.gap: The verbal nouns are not lexemes of their own, and no root_pattern drill uses them.

phenomena.title: Participles that became nouns
phenomena.what: Because the present is a participle, many agent nouns are simply present-tense forms: מוֹכֵר “sells” → “seller”, רוֹפֵא “doctor”, פּוֹעֵל “worker”, מוֹרֶה “teacher”, and in pi‘el מְקָרֵר “cooler” → “fridge”. Recognising the pattern links nouns to verbs.

examples.note: sells → seller
cools (pi‘el) → fridge
doctor — a pa‘al participle

phenomena.record: derivedFrom: the verb and binyan the noun comes from

model.other: Stored as ordinary nouns, some with a root; no link to the verb.

phenomena.gap: A derivedFrom link (verb lexeme or root + binyan) and a root_family drill.

phenomena.title: Passive, causative and reflexive by binyan
phenomena.what: Voice and valency are expressed by changing the binyan, not by auxiliaries: hif‘il makes causatives (אָכַל → הֶאֱכִיל “fed”), nif‘al, pu‘al and huf‘al passives, hitpa‘el reflexives and reciprocals (הִתְלַבֵּשׁ “got dressed”, הִתְרָאוּ “saw each other”).

examples.note: ate → fed
went in → put in
cooked → was cooked (pu‘al)

phenomena.record: related: links to the same-root verbs in other binyanim with their relation

model.other: binyan is recorded but not its relation to other verbs.

phenomena.gap: Relation links between verbs of one root, a function for voice (passive) and the reflexive (cr.07), and root_pattern drills.

phenomena.title: No antipassive
phenomena.what: There is no verb form that removes or demotes the object to make a transitive verb intransitive. A transitive verb is simply used without an object, and the binyanim that change valency (nif‘al, hitpa‘el) make passives, reflexives and reciprocals, not antipassives.

examples.note: she is reading a book / she is reading: the object is just left out

phenomena.gap: Say it with the binyanim (cr.03, cr.07) for learners whose languages have an antipassive.

phenomena.title: No applicative: beneficiaries and tools with prepositions
phenomena.what: No verb affix adds a beneficiary, place or instrument as a new object. They are introduced by prepositions — לְ “for, to”, בִּשְׁבִיל “for”, בְּ “with (a tool)” — and the verb stays the same.

examples.note: I cooked soup for you
I wrote with a pen

phenomena.title: No particle verbs
phenomena.what: Verb meanings are not changed by particles or detachable prefixes. A different meaning is a different root or binyan (יָצָא “went out”, הוֹצִיא “took out”, נִכְנַס “went in”), or a verb with its fixed preposition, which belongs to the complement and stays before its noun.

examples.note: went out / went in: two different verbs, no particle
took out the rubbish: hif‘il of the root of יָצָא

phenomena.title: Few light-verb expressions
phenomena.what: New verbs are made from roots and patterns (טִלְפֵּן “phoned”, סִמֵּס “texted”), not by noun + “do”. Only a handful of colloquial expressions use עָשָׂה “did” or נָתַן “gave” with a noun.

examples.note: he texted (from SMS): a new verb in a pattern
took a shower: one of the few light-verb expressions

phenomena.title: No separable verb-object compounds
phenomena.what: A verb and its object never form one word that other words can split: they are two words, and modifiers go on the object noun in ordinary syntax.

examples.note: we had breakfast: verb + object noun
he sang a nice song: the adjective goes with the noun

phenomena.title: Adjectives: four forms and the article
phenomena.what: An adjective has masculine and feminine, singular and plural forms (גָּדוֹל, גְּדוֹלָה, גְּדוֹלִים, גְּדוֹלוֹת) and takes the article when its noun is definite. The few invariable words (בְּסֵדֶר) are exceptions.

examples.note: big: m. sg, f. sg, m. pl, f. pl

phenomena.record: the 8 ADJ cells

model.other: Required 8 cells for every ADJ; class ADJ.inv for בְּסֵדֶר.

phenomena.title: Adjective patterns: colours and -ִי
phenomena.what: Adjectives also have patterns: colours share קָטֹל (אָדֹם, כָּחֹל, יָרֹק → אֲדֻמָּה, כְּחֻלָּה), and the suffix -ִי makes adjectives from nouns and names (סִין → סִינִי “Chinese”).

examples.note: red (m. → f.) — the colour pattern
China → Chinese

phenomena.record: pattern of the adjective (קָטֹל, קָטוּל, מְקֻטָּל …) or none with the reason

model.other: pattern on every adjective (35 of 45 with a pattern; one-syllable adjectives and suffix forms say none) and the root on 43; fn.comparison teaches the colour pattern and drills colours.

phenomena.gap: The ־ִי derivation when nationality and language words come.

phenomena.title: Reduplication: small and -ish
phenomena.alsoNote: Reduplication in general is common; repeating the last two root consonants for diminutives and '-ish' adjectives is Hebrew's own.
phenomena.what: Repeating the last two root letters makes diminutives and weakened adjectives: קָטָן → קְטַנְטַן “tiny”, אָדֹם → אֲדַמְדַּם “reddish”, בָּצָל → בְּצַלְצַל “shallot (little onion)”.

examples.note: onion → shallot
small → tiny
red → reddish

phenomena.record: pattern / derivedFrom

model.other: בְּצַלְצַל states root ב צ ל and the pattern קְטַלְטַל; גַּרְגִּיר the root ג ר ג ר.

phenomena.gap: derivedFrom links (בְּצַלְצַל ← בָּצָל), the reduplicated colour adjectives (אֲדַמְדַּם) and a note on the colour page.

phenomena.title: No noun incorporation
phenomena.what: An object is never built into the verb word: it stays a separate noun phrase after the verb (with אֶת when definite). New verbs are formed from roots and patterns (טִלְפֵּן “phoned” from טֶלֶפוֹן), not by fusing a noun into a verb.

examples.note: he is reading a newspaper: the object is a separate word
we drank coffee

phenomena.title: Comparison with words, not endings
phenomena.what: Adjectives have no comparative or superlative forms: “bigger” is גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר (or יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל), the standard of comparison takes מִ “from” (or מֵאֲשֶׁר before a clause), and “the most” is הֲכִי (everyday) or בְּיוֹתֵר after the adjective (formal). There are no irregular forms.

examples.note: bigger than the flat
the best

model.other: fn.comparison (periphrastic) with bank sentences.

phenomena.title: Adverbs from prepositions and adjectives
phenomena.alsoNote: Arabic makes adverbs with بِ + noun (بِسُرْعَة, بِصَرَاحَة) in the same way, but uses the accusative of an adjective (جَيِّدًا) where Hebrew uses the bare masculine form; German uses the bare adjective as an adverb.
phenomena.what: Many adverbs are בְּ + a noun (בְּקָרוֹב “soon”, בֶּאֱמֶת “really”, בְּשִׂמְחָה “gladly”), and the masculine singular adjective serves as an adverb (הוּא מְדַבֵּר יָפֶה “he speaks nicely”). The formal pattern is בְּאֹפֶן + adjective.

examples.note: soon (in + near)
really (in + truth)
he speaks nicely

phenomena.record: derivedFrom for adverbs built on a noun or adjective

model.other: derivedFrom on every adverb (18 of 40 built from a preposition, the article or a participle: בְּ + אֱמֶת, הַ + יוֹם, the pu‘al participle of א־ח־ר …; basic adverbs say none).

phenomena.gap: Links to the lexemes of the parts and a short note in the adjective function.

phenomena.title: Numbers with gender — and the reversed endings of 3–10
phenomena.alsoNote: Arabic numerals 3–10 show the same reversed gender agreement; Arabic adds case and a singular noun after 11–99.
phenomena.what: Numbers 1–19 have a masculine and a feminine form, chosen by the counted noun — and for 3–10 the form in -ָה goes with masculine nouns (שְׁלוֹשָׁה סְפָרִים, שָׁלוֹשׁ מִטּוֹת). Plain counting, prices and the clock use the feminine. One follows its noun; every other number precedes it, and the noun is plural. Two and 3–10 have construct forms before a noun or a definite noun (שְׁנֵי, שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַ…). Everyday speech increasingly uses the feminine forms with masculine nouns too, which the norm counts as an error.

examples.note: three books (m.) / three beds (f.)
the three books
one book / two books

phenomena.record: the gender forms and construct forms of each number (class gender / two / const / dual)

model.other: language.json classes NUM.gender, NUM.two, NUM.const, NUM.dual with their cells; fn.numerals with traps; bank variants Gender, Definiteness.

phenomena.gap: The colloquial levelling to feminine forms is not described (register note); the number_words drill (digits ↔ words) is not implemented.

phenomena.title: Twenty-one is “twenty and one”
phenomena.what: From 21 on, the tens come first and the units follow with וְ “and”: עֶשְׂרִים וְאַחַת. Hundreds and thousands also come first. The teens are unit + “ten” (אַחַת־עֶשְׂרֵה), with the gender of the counted noun.

examples.note: 11: in the teens the unit comes first

phenomena.gap: fn.numerals teaches the numbers up to the course's needs; larger compound numbers come later (numbers II).

phenomena.title: Large numbers by thousands
phenomena.what: Large numbers are grouped by thousands: אֶלֶף 1,000, מִילְיוֹן 1,000,000, מִילְיַארְד 10⁹. 2,000 is a dual (אַלְפַּיִם), 3,000–10,000 are the construct numeral + אֲלָפִים (שְׁלוֹשֶׁת אֲלָפִים), and above that the number + אֶלֶף (עֶשְׂרִים אֶלֶף). Digits are grouped in threes.

examples.note: 2,000 — a dual

phenomena.gap: Not yet in the course (numbers II).

phenomena.title: Ordinals only up to ten
phenomena.alsoNote: Ordinals only up to ten, with cardinals after the noun from 11 on, is specific to Hebrew; Arabic has ordinals for higher numbers too.
phenomena.what: Ordinal numbers exist only from 1 to 10 (רִאשׁוֹן, שֵׁנִי, שְׁלִישִׁי … עֲשִׂירִי) and agree like adjectives. From 11 on, the cardinal number with the article follows the noun: הַיּוֹם הָעֶשְׂרִים “the twentieth day”. The weekday names are built on the ordinals.

examples.note: first, second, third
the twentieth day — above ten, a cardinal with the article

model.other: cr.04: the ten ordinals and אַחֲרוֹן as ADJ lexemes with all 8 cells; fn.ordinals explains agreement, the article, the pattern קְטִילִי, the weekdays and the cardinal with the article above ten.

phenomena.gap: Above ten the cardinal with the article (הַיּוֹם הָעֶשְׂרִים) is explained but cannot be in the bank: the cardinals of fd.05 have no form with the article (a DEF cell or an article prefix token is needed).

phenomena.title: Clock, date and age
phenomena.alsoNote: Only the half-hour expression is tagged; feminine numbers for the clock and age as 'son / daughter of' + number are Hebrew's own (literary Arabic ابن عشر سنين is a partial parallel).
phenomena.what: The clock uses feminine numbers because שָׁעָה is feminine (הַשָּׁעָה שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִי), the date is the day + בְּ + month (עֶשְׂרִים בְּמַאי), and age is “son / daughter of” + a feminine number, because שָׁנִים is feminine: הוּא בֶּן שָׁלוֹשׁ.

examples.note: it is half past three
20 May
he is three (years old)

model.other: fn.prep.time (fd.15: hours, months) and fn.numerals (age); cr.04 (fn.ordinals) adds dates as masculine cardinal + בְּ + month (אַרְבָּעָה בְּיוּלִי), minutes with וְ, רֶבַע לְ… and חֲצִי / רֶבַע שָׁעָה, with bank sentences and a quiz.

phenomena.gap: שָׁלוֹשׁ וָחֵצִי / שָׁלוֹשׁ וָרֶבַע are taught in fn.ordinals but cannot be in the bank: the conjunction וְ (fd.01) has no variant וָ among its alts.

phenomena.title: No “to be” in the present
phenomena.what: A present-tense sentence about what something is, what it is like or where it is has no verb: אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט “I (am) a student”, הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל “the house (is) big”, הוּא בַּבַּיִת “he (is) at home”. Identity, quality and location are built the same way, and adjectives do not conjugate. Between two nouns a pronoun agreeing with the subject can stand in for “is” (יֶלֶד הוּא אָדָם). הָיָה appears in the past and future.

examples.note: I am a student
a child is a person — the pronoun as copula

model.other: fn.copula; he:haya has class copula (VERB.copula cells, no present); he:hu / he:hi have a copula sense; bank frames fr.be.person, fr.be.where.

phenomena.title: “There is to me”: יֵשׁ / אֵין + לְ
phenomena.what: There is no verb “have”: יֵשׁ לִי אָח is “there is to me a brother”. The negative is אֵין. In the past and future הָיָה agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner (הָיְתָה לִי דִּירָה).

examples.note: I have a brother
I had a flat — the verb agrees with the flat

model.other: fn.have (periphrastic); he:yesh, he:ein, he:le with its pronoun paradigm.

phenomena.title: אֶת before a definite direct object
phenomena.alsoNote: Persian را and the Turkish accusative mark only definite / specific direct objects, as אֶת does; Hindi-Urdu को and Spanish personal a mark objects partly by animacy (partial).
phenomena.what: A definite direct object is introduced by אֶת, a word with no meaning of its own: הוּא אוֹכֵל אֶת הַתַּפּוּחַ, but הוּא אוֹכֵל תַּפּוּחַ. With a pronoun it becomes אוֹתִי, אוֹתְךָ, אוֹתוֹ … The subject of a transitive verb and of an intransitive verb are treated alike (no marker, verb agreement); only the definite object is marked.

examples.text: הוּא אוֹכֵל תַּפּוּחַ / הוּא אוֹכֵל אֶת הַתַּפּוּחַ
examples.translit: hu okhel tapuach / hu okhel et hatapuach
examples.note: he eats an apple / the apple
I love him / I like it

model.other: he:et (role); fn.object with a Definiteness variant in the bank.

phenomena.gap: The pronoun forms אוֹתִי … אוֹתָן are not stored (see he.morph.prep-suffix); the colloquial אֶת after יֵשׁ (יֵשׁ לִי אֶת הַסֵּפֶר) is mentioned only as non-standard.

phenomena.title: Word order: SVO, modifiers after the noun
phenomena.what: The neutral order is subject – verb – object, and phrases of place, time and manner usually follow the verb and the object. Adjectives, demonstratives and possessives follow the noun; numbers precede it (except אֶחָד). Questions and subordinate clauses keep the same order. Formal and narrative style may put the verb before the subject after an opening adverb or object.

examples.note: the little boy eats the bread
then the teacher said … — verb before subject (formal narration)

model.other: Order taught across the functions; build_sentence takes the bank text and its alts as answers.

phenomena.gap: Verb–subject inversion (literary) is not taught; alts for free orders (time words, יוֹתֵר before or after) depend on each sentence.

phenomena.title: No verb-second rule
phenomena.what: The finite verb has no fixed second position. After a fronted time word or object the subject usually stays before the verb; in formal and narrative style the verb may come before the subject, but this is optional. Subordinate clauses keep the main-clause order.

examples.note: yesterday Dana went to the sea: the subject before the verb
the same, in formal or narrative order

phenomena.title: Built around the subject; topics fronted with a pronoun
phenomena.what: Sentences are organised around a grammatical subject, with which the verb agrees. A topic can still be put first and taken up again with a pronoun, which is very common in speech: הַסֵּפֶר הַזֶּה, קָרָאתִי אוֹתוֹ “this book, I've read it”.

examples.note: this book, I've read it
Dana, her father is a doctor

phenomena.gap: Topic fronting with a resumptive pronoun is not taught yet.

phenomena.title: Agreement in gender and number
phenomena.what: Verbs, adjectives, demonstratives and pronouns agree with the noun's gender and number; a mixed group is masculine. Plural nouns for things take plural agreement, like plural nouns for people (הַסְּפָרִים הָאֵלֶּה, הֵם).

examples.note: the bed was there (f.)
these books — plural things, plural agreement

model.other: fn.agreement; bank variants Gender and Number.

phenomena.title: The article repeated on the adjective
phenomena.what: An adjective or demonstrative after a definite noun takes the article too: הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל “the big house”. Without it the same words form a sentence: הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל “the house is big”.

examples.note: the big house / the house is big
this boy

model.other: DEF cells of adjectives and demonstratives; bank variant Definiteness.

phenomena.title: Subject pronouns: needed in the present, optional in past and future
phenomena.what: Because the present tense shows no person, the pronoun is required (אֲנִי אוֹכֵל). In the past and future the 1st and 2nd person endings show the person and the pronoun is usually left out (אָכַלְתִּי); in the 3rd person it is normally kept.

examples.note: (I) ate — pronoun optional / I eat — pronoun required

model.other: Taught in fn.pronoun.subject, fn.copula and fn.present (traps).

phenomena.title: Impersonal sentences: “they call me”, “cold to me”
phenomena.alsoNote: Russian, Ukrainian and Polish have the same three constructions: a subjectless 3rd person plural ('they say'), a dative experiencer with an invariable predicative (мне холодно, zimno mi) and impersonal modals + infinitive (надо, можно, trzeba). German mir ist kalt is a partial parallel.
phenomena.what: A masculine plural verb without subject means “people, one” (קוֹרְאִים לִי דָּנָה “my name is Dana”). Feelings and states take לְ + the person and an unchanging masculine singular adjective (קַר לִי “I'm cold”, קָשֶׁה לִי “it's hard for me”). Modals such as צָרִיךְ, אֶפְשָׁר, אָסוּר + infinitive are impersonal too.

examples.note: my name is Dana (they call me Dana)
I'm cold
smoking is forbidden

phenomena.record: governs/impersonal use of the adjective or verb

model.other: he:korim-li is a fixed phrase; fn.adjective mentions חַם לִי / קַר לִי; the modals are not yet in the course.

phenomena.gap: A note or function on impersonal constructions, the dative-experiencer use marked on the adjectives that allow it, and the modals (cr.04).

phenomena.title: Relative clauses with שֶׁ and a resumptive pronoun
phenomena.alsoNote: Arabic and Persian also take a resumptive pronoun inside the relative clause; the Arabic relativizer agrees (الذي، التي) and is left out after an indefinite head.
phenomena.what: Relative clauses start with the invariable שֶׁ (formal אֲשֶׁר). When the noun is not the subject or object, a pronoun points back to it inside the clause: הַבַּיִת שֶׁאֲנִי גָּר בּוֹ “the house I live in (it)”. Prepositions are never left at the end.

examples.note: the house I live in
the book that I bought

model.other: he:she has the relative sense s2; no function yet (cr.06 is planned).

phenomena.gap: The cr.06 realization (שֶׁ, אֲשֶׁר, resumptive pronouns, ה־ + participle in formal style) and bank sentences.

phenomena.title: No serial verbs
phenomena.what: Bare verbs are not strung together in one clause to express direction, instrument, purpose or result: the second verb is an infinitive, the clauses are joined with וְ, or a preposition does the job.

examples.note: he cut the bread with a knife: a preposition, not a second verb
I went to buy bread: the second verb is an infinitive

phenomena.title: No switch reference
phenomena.what: A dependent verb does not show whether its subject is the same as that of the main verb. The person endings or a pronoun say who does what, and with the same subject an infinitive is used where possible (בָּאתִי כְּדֵי לַעֲזֹר “I came to help”).

examples.note: when I arrived, I ate
when she arrived, he left: the pronouns show the change of subject

phenomena.gap: Say it in the overview for learners whose languages have switch reference.

phenomena.title: Subordinate clauses: שֶׁ, no word-order change
phenomena.what: Subordinate clauses are finite clauses introduced by a conjunction, and they keep main-clause order: the verb does not move. “That” (שֶׁ) is written onto the next word and is never left out; preposition + שֶׁ makes a conjunction (לִפְנֵי שֶׁ, אַחֲרֵי שֶׁ, לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ). Reported speech keeps its tense, and future events after כְּשֶׁ / אִם are in the future.

examples.note: I know that he is here — שֶׁ cannot be dropped
when I grow up — future after כְּשֶׁ

model.other: fn.connectors with traps and bank sentences.

phenomena.title: No converbs: clauses joined with conjunctions
phenomena.what: There is no non-finite verb form meaning “having done” or “while doing” for chaining clauses. Every clause has its own finite verb, joined by וְ “and”, כְּשֶׁ “when”, אַחֲרֵי שֶׁ “after”, or a preposition + verbal noun (אַחֲרֵי הָאֲרוּחָה “after the meal”).

examples.note: I got up, got dressed and went out: three finite verbs
when I arrived, he had already left

phenomena.title: Questions without inversion
phenomena.what: Yes/no questions keep statement order and rise in intonation; formal writing may open them with the particle הַאִם. Question words go first; a preposition goes with the question word (עִם מִי?) and is never stranded. No auxiliary verb is added and the verb does not move.

examples.note: do you want coffee?
who are you with?

model.other: fn.question.yesno and fn.question.wh; bank variants Mood, QuestionMarker.

phenomena.title: Negation: לֹא, אֵין and negative concord
phenomena.what: לֹא, placed before the verb or predicate, negates it; אֵין negates existence and possession in the present (and formally the verbless sentence). Negative words need לֹא as well (אַף אֶחָד לֹא …). Commands are negated with אַל.

examples.note: I have no time
nobody eats

model.other: fn.negation; bank variant Polarity.

phenomena.title: Verbs and adjectives with their own preposition
phenomena.what: Each verb takes a fixed preposition or אֶת, which must be learned with it: חִכָּה לְ “wait for”, נִכְנַס לְ “go into”, יָצָא מִ “go out of”, עָזַב אֶת “leave”, עָזַר לְ “help”, פָּחַד מִ “be afraid of”; adjectives too: קָרוֹב לְ “close to”, רָחוֹק מִ “far from”. All of them are prepositions, standing before their noun.

examples.note: waits for the bus
leaves the city / goes out of the city

phenomena.record: governs: the preposition (or אֶת) each meaning takes, for every verb and adjective (none for an adjective without a complement)

model.other: governs on all 19 verbs (each meaning: אֶת, לְ, בְּ, מִ, עַל, עִם or none) and on every adjective (7 with a complement: קָרוֹב לְ, רָחוֹק מִ, עָיֵף מִ, רָעֵב לְ …); also in grammar traps (fn.direction, fn.prep.place).

phenomena.gap: A drill (choose the preposition) and the case frames of the nouns.

phenomena.title: Where, where to, where from — and the directional -ָה
phenomena.what: Place, goal and source are three prepositions (בְּ, לְ, מִ) and three question words (אֵיפֹה, לְאָן, מֵאֵיפֹה). A few words keep an old ending -ָה “towards”: הַבַּיְתָה “home(wards)”, הַחוּצָה “out”, שְׂמֹאלָה “to the left”.

examples.note: home(wards)
to the left / on the left

model.other: he:habayta and he:lean are lexemes; the other -ָה forms appear only in grammar texts.

phenomena.gap: Lexemes for הַחוּצָה, פְּנִימָה, שְׂמֹאלָה, יָמִינָה, מֵאֵיפֹה.

phenomena.title: Direction in the verb: נִכְנַס, יָצָא, עָלָה, יָרַד
phenomena.what: Motion verbs usually name the path: נִכְנַס “go in”, יָצָא “go out”, עָלָה “go up”, יָרַד “go down”, עָבַר “cross”, חָזַר “go back”. The manner, if said at all, is added with a phrase (בְּרִיצָה “at a run”); verbs of manner (רָץ “run”) take a preposition for the goal.

examples.note: he went into the house
she ran out — “went out at a run”
we went up the stairs

phenomena.title: Where things are: no posture verbs needed
phenomena.what: The location of a thing is stated with no verb in the present (הַסֵּפֶר עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן “the book is on the table”), with נִמְצָא “is located”, or with יֵשׁ “there is”; past and future use הָיָה. Posture verbs (עוֹמֵד “stands”, שׁוֹכֵב “lies”, יוֹשֵׁב “sits”) describe people and animals, and things only for emphasis.

examples.note: the book is on the table: no verb
where is the bank?

phenomena.gap: fn.prep.place now says that a location needs no verb, not even a posture verb; נִמְצָא “is located” is not taught yet.

phenomena.title: Three tenses, no grammatical aspect; habitual with הָיָה
phenomena.what: Every finite verb is in one of three tenses — past, present or future — and the tense must be chosen. There is no grammatical aspect: no perfective / imperfective pair and no progressive, so אֲנִי אוֹכֵל is “I eat” and “I am eating”, and one past form covers a finished event and an ongoing one. A habitual or repeated past is הָיָה + the present form: הָיִיתִי הוֹלֵךְ “I used to go”.

examples.note: I eat / I am eating
I used to go to the sea

model.other: fn.present and fn.past state that one form covers simple, progressive and perfect meanings; cr.02 (fn.past.ongoing, periphrastic) teaches הָיָה + present for habits and backgrounds, with Aspect variants (plain past ↔ habitual) in the bank, and נָהַג + infinitive as the formal alternative; comparison notes for el and ru (aspect).

phenomena.title: No perfect: the simple past does the job
phenomena.what: There is no form for “has done”: the simple past serves both for a finished event and for a result that matters now, often with כְּבָר “already” or עוֹד לֹא “not yet”. A state lasting until now is in the present with a time phrase.

examples.note: I have already eaten: the simple past
I have lived here for a year: the present

model.other: fn.past (cr.01) says that קַמְתִּי is also “I have got up” and carries the verb.perfect = none tag, with notes for the languages that have a perfect.

phenomena.title: No subjunctive: the future after שֶׁ
phenomena.what: There is no special mood for wishes, purposes or requests in subordinate clauses: they use the future after שֶׁ or כְּדֵי שֶׁ “so that”. With the same subject the infinitive is used.

examples.note: I want you to come — “that you will come”
I want to come — the same subject: the infinitive

model.other: fn.future (cr.03) says that the future is the verb after שֶׁ in wishes and requests (אֲנִי רוֹצֶה שֶׁתְּבַקֵּר אוֹתָנוּ) and after אַל in prohibitions; the bank of fd.18 has אִמָּא רוֹצָה שֶׁתֹּאכַל.

phenomena.gap: The choice between שֶׁ + future (another subject) and the infinitive (the same subject) is not drilled yet; the conditional comes later.

phenomena.title: No optative: wishes with הַלְוַאי or the future
phenomena.what: No verb form is reserved for wishes. Wishes use הַלְוַאי (שֶׁ) “if only” + a verb, the ordinary future in blessings (תִּהְיֶה בָּרִיא, תִּתְחַדֵּשׁ), or a noun phrase (רְפוּאָה שְׁלֵמָה, מַזָּל טוֹב).

examples.note: if only it would rain
be healthy (bless you) — the future as a wish

phenomena.gap: fn.greetings now says that the wishes are ordinary phrases (בֹּקֶר טוֹב, the infinitive לְהִתְרָאוֹת); הַלְוַאי “if only” is not taught yet.

phenomena.title: No evidentials: the source is said in words
phenomena.what: The verb does not show whether the speaker saw the event, inferred it or heard about it. When the source matters it is said in words: כַּנִּרְאֶה “apparently”, שָׁמַעְתִּי שֶׁ… “I heard that”, לְפִי… “according to”, אוֹמְרִים שֶׁ… “they say that”.

examples.note: he went to Eilat: the same form whether seen or heard
I heard he went to Eilat

phenomena.title: No mirative: surprise by intonation and words
phenomena.what: Nothing in the verb marks new or surprising information. Surprise is carried by intonation and by words such as וָאוּ, מָה?!, אֵיזֶה … ! “what a …!” or פִּתְאוֹם “suddenly”.

examples.note: he's here?! — intonation only
how lovely!

phenomena.title: Real and unreal conditions
phenomena.what: Real conditions use אִם with the future (or present); unreal ones use לוּ / אִלּוּ with the past (or הָיָה + the present form), and הָיָה + the present form in the main clause: אִלּוּ הָיָה לִי כֶּסֶף, הָיִיתִי קוֹנֶה. There is no subjunctive mood.

examples.note: if it rains, we'll stay at home

examples.text: אִלּוּ הָיָה לִי כֶּסֶף, הָיִיתִי קוֹנֶה
examples.translit: ilu haya li kesef, hayiti kone
examples.note: if I had money, I would buy

model.other: fn.connectors covers real אִם + future; unreal conditions are not taught.

phenomena.gap: The cr.05 realization with לוּ / אִלּוּ and bank sentences.

phenomena.title: The article meaning “this”: הַיּוֹם, הַבֹּקֶר
phenomena.what: With time words the article means “this”: הַיּוֹם “today” (the day), הַבֹּקֶר “this morning”, הַלַּיְלָה “tonight”, הַשָּׁנָה “this year”.

examples.note: today / this morning / tonight

model.other: he:hayom is a lexeme; fn.time.day explains הַבֹּקֶר / הָעֶרֶב / הַלַּיְלָה; senses s2 of he:boker and he:laila.

phenomena.title: כָּל: “all” or “every” by definiteness
phenomena.what: כָּל before a definite noun means “all, the whole” and before an indefinite singular noun “every”: כָּל הַיּוֹם “the whole day”, כָּל יוֹם “every day”. Alone it takes personal endings: כֻּלָּם “everyone”, כֻּלָּנוּ “all of us”.

examples.note: the whole day / every day
everyone, all of them

model.other: he:kol senses (all / every / any); he:kulam with class PRON.all; no grammar function teaches the definiteness rule.

phenomena.gap: A short rule (fn.numerals or a quantifier note) and bank sentences contrasting כָּל הַ… / כָּל ….

phenomena.title: Everyday concepts split by manner and object
phenomena.what: Several everyday concepts are split into separate words: going on foot or by vehicle (הָלַךְ / נָסַע), leaving a place or leaving something behind (יָצָא / עָזַב), and above all “wearing”: clothes, shoes and hats each have their own verb (לָבַשׁ, נָעַל, חָבַשׁ). See “distinctions” for the full list.

examples.text: לָבַשׁ חֻלְצָה / נָעַל נַעֲלַיִם / חָבַשׁ כּוֹבַע
examples.translit: lavash chultsa / na'al na'alayim / chavash kova
examples.note: put on a shirt / shoes / a hat
go on foot / go by vehicle

phenomena.record: the words of one concept say what separates them (contrasts: one axis per concept, a value per word); the sense split is recorded per sense

model.other: 79 concepts have two or more Hebrew words, each with its contrast (one axis per concept: addressee, register, place or direction …; the distinctions list below is generated from them); sense_split and nuance_pick (§6.2) are not implemented.

phenomena.gap: The sense_split exercise, and the splits not yet in the course (wear, play, know, ask, time).

phenomena.title: Two verbs of knowing: יָדַע and הִכִּיר
phenomena.what: יָדַע “know” takes facts, clauses and skills (אֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ לִשְׂחוֹת “I can swim”); הִכִּיר “know, be acquainted with” takes people, places and things one is familiar with. See “distinctions”.

examples.note: I know where he lives
I know Dana

phenomena.gap: Not yet in the course: teach יָדַע / הִכִּיר as a pair.

phenomena.title: One general verb for carrying
phenomena.what: Carrying is one verb whatever the manner — formal נָשָׂא, everyday סָחַב (also “lug, drag”) — in the hand, on the back or on the shoulder alike; the manner can be added with a phrase (עַל הַגַּב “on the back”). “Bring” (הֵבִיא) and “take” (לָקַח) are separate verbs of direction.

examples.note: he is carrying a heavy bag

examples.text: הִיא סוֹחֶבֶת אֶת הַיֶּלֶד עַל הַגַּב
examples.translit: hi sokhevet et hayeled al hagav
examples.note: she carries the child on her back: the same verb, the manner as a phrase

phenomena.gap: Not yet in the course.

phenomena.title: A general verb “cut”
phenomena.what: חָתַךְ “cut” is used with a knife, scissors or anything else. More specific verbs exist for particular ways of cutting — גָּזַר “cut out (with scissors)”, קָצַץ “chop”, פָּרַס “slice” — but they are not required.

examples.note: I cut the bread
I cut the paper with scissors: the same verb

phenomena.gap: Not yet in the course.

phenomena.title: One word, several meanings — and homographs
phenomena.alsoNote: The particular polysemies are Hebrew's own; German bitte and Russian пожалуйста also mean both 'please' and 'you're welcome'.
phenomena.what: Many basic words cover several concepts: אָח is a brother and a male nurse, בַּעַל a husband and an owner, בְּבַקָּשָׁה both “please” and “you're welcome”. The unvocalized script adds homographs on top. See “polysemy” for the course words.

examples.note: brother; (male) nurse
husband; owner

phenomena.record: profile.senses: every distinct meaning with its concept (pending if the course does not teach it yet) or “of” the meaning it is a nuance of; meaningForms (and the items of plurals, dual, construct) name the meanings their forms belong to

model.other: Every profile sense has a concept or of (D15); 26 words state forms that belong to some meanings only (meaningForms); the polysemy list below is generated from the lexicon. The sense_pick exercise is not implemented.

phenomena.gap: sense_pick from profile examples labelled by sense.

phenomena.title: Registers: everyday, formal and the old layers
phenomena.alsoNote: Modern Greek likewise keeps learned words of older stages beside everyday ones within one standard (ύδωρ / νερό, οίκος / σπίτι). Russian Church Slavonic doublets (глава / голова) and English Latinate words are partial parallels.
phenomena.what: Modern Hebrew is one standard language — speech and writing share the same grammar — but it keeps Biblical and Mishnaic words beside everyday ones, so many concepts have a formal and an everyday word: אִמָּא / אֵם, לָמָּה / מַדּוּעַ, פֹּה / כָּאן, קוֹרְאִים לִי / שְׁמִי, אֲנִי לֹא / אֵינֶנִּי. Writing, news and formal speech use the formal layer much more than conversation.

examples.note: mum (everyday) / mother (formal)
why (everyday / formal)
I am not (everyday / literary)

phenomena.record: profile.register and synonyms with register and nuance

model.other: profile.register on every content word; synonyms with register; bank variant Formality.

phenomena.gap: register_pick (§6.2) is not implemented; the inflected formal negation אֵינִי / אֵינוֹ … is recorded on אֵין (meaningForms) but not stored as cells.

phenomena.title: Loanwords and slang
phenomena.alsoNote: The mix of loans and slang is Hebrew's own; Arabic speakers recognise the Arabic slang (יאללה, סבבה), Russian and English speakers some of the rest.
phenomena.what: Everyday Hebrew is full of international loans (סְטוּדֶנְט, טֶלֶפוֹן, אוֹטוֹבּוּס) and slang from Arabic, Yiddish, English and Russian: יאללה “come on!” comes from Arabic. Loans keep their foreign sounds (no b/v alternation) and usually have no Semitic root.

examples.note: come on, let's go — from Arabic
international loans

phenomena.record: profile.etymology (source language), root “none (loan)”

model.other: profile.etymology on every profiled word; root and pattern of a loanword say none, naming the source (a loanword (Greek χάρτης) …); fn.root.pattern notes loans have no root.

phenomena.gap: bridges.json (cognates and loans across the course and known languages, §4.10) and slang lexemes with register.

phenomena.title: Compounds made of two nouns
phenomena.what: New concepts are rarely one compound word; many everyday nouns are construct pairs written as two words: בֵּית סֵפֶר “school”, בֵּית חוֹלִים “hospital”, עוֹרֵךְ דִּין “lawyer”, יוֹם הֻלֶּדֶת “birthday”. They inflect as a construct pair: the plural changes the first word, the article goes on the second. A few blends are written as one word (רַמְזוֹר “traffic light”, from רֶמֶז + אוֹר).

examples.note: hospital → hospitals
lawyer → lawyers

phenomena.record: the compound's parts (lexeme ids) and its forms

model.other: Stored as multi-word lexemes with complete forms (ארוחת הבוקר with the inner article); the tokenizer reads multi-word lexemes. Their facade says root, pattern and construct: none — a compound of two words, naming the parts.

phenomena.gap: A parts link to the member nouns and the construct rule taught (see he.morph.construct).

phenomena.title: בֶּן, בַּת, בַּעַל + noun
phenomena.what: בֶּן / בַּת “son / daughter of” and בַּעַל “owner of”, in their construct forms, make many words and expressions of belonging, age and quality: בֶּן אָדָם “person”, בֶּן זוּג “partner”, בֶּן שֵׁשׁ “six years old”, בַּעַל נִסָּיוֹן “experienced”.

examples.note: person (son of Adam)
partner (m. / f.)
she is six

model.other: Senses with their concepts on he:ben, he:bat, he:baal; their construct forms (בֶּן / בְּנֵי, בַּת / בְּנוֹת, בַּעַל / בַּעֲלֵי) are cells and facade items; meaningForms says which meanings use only the construct (בֶּן שֵׁשׁ, בֶּן אָדָם) and which only the plural (בָּנִים “boys”).

phenomena.title: Kinship words
phenomena.what: Uncles and aunts are not split by side of the family (דּוֹד, דּוֹדָה for both), cousins are built from them (בֶּן דּוֹד “uncle's son”), and there is a word for the parents of one's child's spouse, מְחֻתָּן / מְחֻתֶּנֶת. Everyday family words have a name-like form used without the article (אִמָּא, אַבָּא, סַבָּא, סָבְתָא).

examples.note: uncle — on the father's or the mother's side
cousin (uncle's son)
father / mother of one's child's spouse

model.other: The family field (fd.06) is complete for blood relatives; in-laws (חָמִי, חֲמוֹתִי, גִּיס, גִּיסָה, מְחֻתָּן) are not in the course.

phenomena.gap: An in-laws group in a later family field, and a note on name-like use without the article.

phenomena.title: Brothers and sisters without relative age
phenomena.what: אָח “brother” and אָחוֹת “sister” do not say whether the sibling is older or younger; when it matters, an adjective is added: אָח גָּדוֹל “older (big) brother”, אָחוֹת קְטַנָּה “younger (little) sister”.

examples.note: older brother — “big brother”
younger sister — “little sister”

phenomena.title: Look-alike words with another meaning
phenomena.alsoNote: The false friends are specific to Hebrew.
phenomena.what: Some Hebrew words look like international words but are built from Hebrew roots or have taken another meaning: קַנְיוֹן is a shopping mall (from קָנָה “buy” + the noun ending -יוֹן), not a canyon; פְּרוֹטֶקְצְיָה is pulling strings, not “protection”. A word that sounds familiar must be checked.

examples.note: shopping mall — not a canyon
connections, pulling strings — not protection

model.other: Only as pitfalls in individual profiles; no bridges.json.

phenomena.gap: bridges.json with kind falseFriend (§4.10) and the cognate_bridge exercise.

phenomena.title: Roots shared with the other Semitic languages
phenomena.what: Hebrew shares thousands of roots with the other Semitic languages — Arabic, Aramaic, Amharic, Maltese and others — often with regular sound correspondences: שָׁלוֹם ~ Arabic سَلَام, בַּיִת ~ بَيْت, יוֹם ~ يَوْم, אָכַל ~ أَكَلَ. Many Semitic words also reached other languages through Arabic and Aramaic, so a root may be recognisable in borrowed words.

examples.note: peace
house
day

model.other: fn.root.pattern names أَكَلَ ~ א־כ־ל; profile.etymology mentions cognates; no bridges.json.

phenomena.gap: bridges.json (kind cognate) between ar and he, and the cognate_bridge exercise.

phenomena.title: Idioms from the Bible and the Talmud
phenomena.alsoNote: The idioms are Hebrew's own; many Biblical idioms exist as calques in European languages (partial).

phenomena.title: Gender in every “you”
phenomena.what: Talking to a man or a woman changes the pronoun (אַתָּה / אַתְּ), the verb, the possessive and many fixed phrases (מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ / מַה שְּׁלוֹמֵךְ, בּוֹא / בּוֹאִי). Mixed groups and generic texts use the masculine; modern writing often shows both with a slash.

examples.note: how are you? (to a man / to a woman)
come! (m. / f.)
students (m./f.) — inclusive slash writing

phenomena.record: addressee: who each greeting or phrase is said to (a man, a woman, several people, anyone)

phenomena.title: The speaker's own gender in “I” sentences
phenomena.what: Speakers mark their own gender whenever a present-tense verb, an adjective or a participle refers to “I”: a man says אֲנִי עָיֵף, a woman אֲנִי עֲיֵפָה. The 1st person forms of the past and future verb are the same for both (אָכַלְתִּי, אֹכַל), but an adjective after הָיִיתִי still agrees.

examples.note: I am tired (a man / a woman)
I am learning Hebrew (a man / a woman)

phenomena.title: One “we”, inclusive or not
phenomena.what: אֲנַחְנוּ “we” is used whether or not the listener is included, with the same verb forms (-נוּ in the past, נ־ in the future); context shows who is meant.

examples.note: we are going to the sea — with or without the listener

phenomena.title: No polite “you”, no speech levels, direct style
phenomena.what: There is no T/V distinction: a friend, a teacher and a minister are all אַתָּה or אַתְּ, often with the first name. Verbs have no honorific or polite forms and no speech levels. Politeness is carried by words (בְּבַקָּשָׁה, תּוֹדָה, סְלִיחָה), by titles (אֲדוֹנִי “sir”, גְּבִרְתִּי “madam”) and by tone; Israeli conversation is known for its directness.

examples.note: the same “you” for a friend and for a minister

model.other: Stated in fn.overview, fn.greetings and fn.pronoun.subject.

phenomena.title: Fixed social and religious formulas
phenomena.alsoNote: The formulas themselves are Hebrew and Jewish; Arabic, Turkish, Persian and Greek have comparable occasion formulas (e.g. religious phrases in everyday Arabic, Turkish güle güle kullan or Greek με γεια for something new).
phenomena.what: Daily life is full of set phrases for occasions: שַׁבָּת שָׁלוֹם on Friday and Saturday, חַג שָׂמֵחַ for holidays, מַזָּל טוֹב “congratulations”, בְּתֵאָבוֹן “enjoy your meal”, לְחַיִּים “cheers”, רְפוּאָה שְׁלֵמָה “get well”, תִּתְחַדֵּשׁ / תִּתְחַדְּשִׁי for something new, and religious ones even in secular speech (בְּעֶזְרַת הַשֵּׁם, בָּרוּךְ הַשֵּׁם). Wishes are noun phrases or the ordinary future (תִּתְחַדֵּשׁ “may you renew yourself”), as there is no special wish form of the verb.

phenomena.title: The Hebrew calendar beside the Gregorian
phenomena.alsoNote: Living with a traditional calendar beside the Gregorian is common; the Hebrew lunisolar calendar (leap Adar, days from sunset) is new to everyone. Hindu calendars are also lunisolar with leap months, and Islamic reckoning also starts the day at sunset.
phenomena.what: Daily life uses the Gregorian months (יָנוּאָר …), but the Hebrew lunisolar calendar fixes the holidays and is used for dates in religious and official contexts: twelve months (תִּשְׁרֵי … אֱלוּל) with a second Adar in leap years, and days that begin at sunset (עֶרֶב שַׁבָּת is Friday evening).

examples.text: תִּשְׁרֵי, נִיסָן, אֲדָר א׳ / אֲדָר ב׳
examples.translit: Tishrei, Nisan, Adar I / Adar II
examples.note: Hebrew months; a leap year has two Adars

phenomena.title: A week of numbered days, starting on Sunday
phenomena.what: The weekdays are numbered: יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן “first day” is Sunday, יוֹם שֵׁנִי Monday … יוֹם שִׁשִּׁי Friday; only שַׁבָּת has a name. The week starts on Sunday and the weekend is Friday–Saturday.

examples.note: Sunday (first day) / Monday (second day)

NOUN.title: gender
NOUN.why: Every agreeing word (adjective, verb, demonstrative, number) depends on it, and the ending often misleads (לַיְלָה m., עִיר f.).

NOUN.title: learner transliteration
NOUN.why: Until the script is learned every word is shown with its romanization, in one scheme: ch for ח and כ, ts for צ, sh for שׁ, ei for ֵי, an apostrophe before an ע / א that opens a syllable inside a word, a hyphen after a prefix (be-, le-).

NOUN.title: everyday spelling (no vowel points)
NOUN.why: Everyday texts are unvocalized: the learner must read and type the standard full spelling (ktiv male), which often adds ו or י to the stripped form (שֻׁלְחָן → שולחן).

NOUN.title: root
NOUN.why: The root letters, separated by spaces (כ ת ב): the root links the word to its family and to cognates in the other Semitic languages. Loans, compounds and primary words say none, with the reason.

NOUN.title: noun pattern (mishkal)
NOUN.why: The pattern, written with the dummy root ק־ט־ל, carries meaning (places מִקְטָל, tools, professions קַטָּל) and predicts the plural and the construct. Loans, compounds and primary or one-syllable nouns say none.

NOUN.title: plural
NOUN.why: The plural is not predictable from the gender (חַלּוֹנוֹת m., שָׁנִים f.) and the stem often changes; a meaning may have its own plural (כִּכָּרוֹת squares, כִּכְּרוֹת loaves).

NOUN.title: dual (“two …”)
NOUN.why: A few nouns (units of time, paired things) say “two” with the ending ־ַיִם (יוֹמַיִם); all others use שְׁנֵי / שְׁתֵּי + the plural.

NOUN.title: construct forms (“the … of”)
NOUN.why: Needed for every “X of Y” phrase and every compound; the stem often changes (בַּיִת → בֵּית, ־ָה → ־ַת, ־ִים → ־ֵי). The forms are also paradigm cells.

NOUN.title: forms of one meaning
NOUN.why: A meaning may use only some forms (only the plural, only the construct, only with the article, only the imperative): each such form names its meanings.
